name: Maritime pine bark extract (Pycnogenol)
lead: Pycnogenol is the trademarked name of a standardised extract of French maritime pine (Pinus pinaster) bark, composed mainly of proanthocyanidins (procyanidins, about 70%).[1][2] The term was coined in 1979 by chemist Jack Masquelier, who had extracted proanthocyanidins from pine bark.[2]

People take it as an antioxidant supplement aimed at skin: the idea is that its polyphenols help limit UV-related and oxidative skin damage, even out pigmentation such as melasma, and support the collagen and elastin framework that keeps skin firm. A 2016 review of its effects on human skin reports clinical and molecular findings for reduced hyperpigmentation, better skin barrier function and extracellular matrix maintenance, beyond photoprotection.[14] A small 2002 trial in women with melasma reported decreases in lesion area and pigment intensity.[13] Laboratory work reports free-radical scavenging and inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases by its metabolites.[3][4]

Beyond skin, it has been studied for many other conditions. A Cochrane review, updated in 2020 and summarised on Wikipedia, examined uses including asthma, ADHD, blood pressure, osteoarthritis and cognition after brain injury, and found insufficient evidence of efficacy; meta-analyses have likewise concluded that evidence is insufficient for any disease.[2] A 2024 review written about the product describes 39 randomised placebo-controlled trials with 2,009 subjects reporting benefits across several health domains including skin health.[15]

paras: Skin is the main appearance interest: pigmentation (melasma and sun-related dark patches), skin barrier function and signs of ageing.[13][14] It is generally taken by mouth as part of an antioxidant or beauty-from-within routine, often alongside vitamin C and similar supplements.

Research has examined circulation and venous insufficiency, blood pressure, joint pain, asthma, ADHD, gum health and cognition.[2][8][9][10][11][15] Chronic venous insufficiency and pregnancy-related pain have been studied in controlled trials.[16][17]

A 2002 review described a diverse pharmacology for the extract, covering antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and vascular actions identified in laboratory and clinical studies.[1] Metabolites of the extract showed antioxidant activity and inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases, enzymes involved in collagen breakdown, in a 2004 study, which is the basis of skin-related interest.[3] Related experiments found that pine-bark polyphenols reduced nitric oxide production and inflammatory signalling in macrophages and increased plasma antioxidant capacity.[5][6]

A 2024 pharmacokinetics review reports that the standardised product contains 65 to 75 percent procyanidins and that small constituents such as catechin, caffeic acid and ferulic acid are absorbed in the small intestine, while larger procyanidins are broken down by gut bacteria into small metabolites that enter the circulation.[18]
Pine bark extracts are also studied outside medicine, for example as natural preservatives in meat.[7]

Skin: a 2002 clinical trial in Phytotherapy Research followed 30 women with melasma for 30 days of daily Pycnogenol; the authors report significant reductions in melasma area and pigment intensity, roughly 80 percent responders, and no side effects.[13] It was a single-group trial. A 2016 review in Skin Pharmacology and Physiology summarises clinical and molecular findings on pigmentation, barrier function and the extracellular matrix.[14] A 2008 review of natural antioxidants in dermatology also discusses the extract.[19]

Other conditions: registered trials cover hypertension (UPBEAT, n=130), arm lymphedema after breast cancer (Phase 2, n=26), ADHD (two studies, n=32 and n=88), gum inflammation (n=90), traumatic brain injury (n=67), mild cognitive impairment and exercise fatigue.[8][9][10][11] A randomised, placebo-controlled 2025 trial examined salivary and serum inflammatory biomarkers during periodontal therapy.[20] A 2018 meta-analysis of supplements for osteoarthritis listed pycnogenol among seven supplements with large short-term effects on pain, while noting limited clinical importance for most supplements over longer periods.[21]

The Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia found insufficient evidence for efficacy across the indications it examined.[2] Many published trials are small, and the 2024 overview of placebo-controlled trials was written about the branded product.[15]

Pycnogenol is sold as a dietary supplement rather than a drug.[2] It also circulates in bodybuilding and hormone-optimisation forums, where members discuss it alongside L-arginine for circulation and erection quality; one forum member noted that a study of the combination did not appear to have been replicated by others.[22]

Masquelier is credited with extracting proanthocyanidins from European maritime pine bark and introducing the name Pycnogenol in 1979, reportedly inspired by an account of bark tea used by Jacques Cartier's expedition.[2]

card.summary: Pine-bark polyphenol antioxidant floated for skin and melasma; Cochrane found insufficient evidence for other uses and no skin trial turned up.
card.aka: Pycnogenol, French maritime pine bark extract
card.note: Skin and melasma claims rest on lab antioxidant data.

quick.overview:
Pycnogenol is a branded extract of French maritime pine bark rich in procyanidins, sold as an antioxidant supplement and mentioned for skin and melasma.
A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for efficacy across the conditions it examined, and no skin or melasma trial exists.
quick.mechanism: Lab studies report free-radical scavenging and inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases by its metabolites, the basis for skin-ageing interest. Human skin effects have not been shown.
quick.risks: It is sold as a dietary supplement, not a drug.

chain: Pine-bark procyanidins act as antioxidants and inhibit collagen-degrading enzymes in lab studies
Less oxidative and UV-linked skin stress, and less pigment in melasma in a small trial
angle.text: People take it as a daily supplement hoping for more even skin tone and better skin quality over time. The appearance case rests on antioxidant and matrix-protecting mechanisms and a small melasma trial.
